summary: Greece lies at the southern end of the Balkan Peninsula, has numerous Aegean islands, and is the birthplace of Western philosophy, democracy and the Olympic Games.

ranking.name: Greek Orthodox Church
ranking.description: In the mid-1st century AD the Apostle Paul preached in Philippi, Thessaloniki, Corinth and Athens, making Greece one of the earliest regions to accept Christianity; the Byzantine Empire, centered on Constantinople, then developed Eastern Orthodoxy. After the Ottoman conquest of 1453 the Orthodox Church was responsible for administering the Greek community, becoming the pillar that preserved language and national consciousness, and it played an important role in the War of Independence of 1821. The current constitution defines Greek Orthodoxy as the "prevailing religion", and Orthodoxy and Greek identity are almost inseparable.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Because religion is closely linked with national identity and public holidays, even people who rarely go to church mostly identify as Orthodox, so the proportion of non-religious people is low by European standards. Those who declare no religion are concentrated among the young and highly educated in cities such as Athens and Thessaloniki, and have increased in recent years with secularization and the social changes after the debt crisis of the 2010s.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 provided for an exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey, but the Muslims of Western Thrace in the north-east were exempted, including Turks, Pomaks and some Roma, who are still guaranteed religious and educational rights by the treaty. After the 1990s, immigrants from Albania, Pakistan, the Middle East and elsewhere also increased the number of Muslims, and Athens did not have its first official mosque until 2020.

religion.background: Greece is one of the earliest regions where Christianity spread, the New Testament was originally written in Greek, and a thousand years of Byzantine rule rooted Eastern Orthodoxy deeply in people's hearts. After 1453 the Ottoman Empire divided its subjects by religion, and the Orthodox Church became the representative institution of the Greeks. After the War of Independence of 1821, the Church of Greece declared itself autocephalous from the Patriarch of Constantinople in 1833 and was recognized in 1850. After the Greek–Turkish population exchange of 1923, Greece became an almost single-religion country, with only Western Thrace retaining a Muslim minority.

ranking.name: Greek
ranking.description: Greek is one of the languages in Europe with the longest written record, which can be traced back to Linear B of the Mycenaean civilization in the 14th–13th centuries BC. Through the Homeric epics, classical Athens, the Koine Greek of Alexander's empire, and the Byzantine period, it has been in continuous use for more than three thousand years. Modern Greece long had a dispute between the archaizing "Katharevousa" (purist language) and the spoken "Demotic", and in 1976 the government formally made Demotic the standard language, and in 1982 the accent marks were simplified.

ranking.name: Albanian
ranking.description: Albanian speakers fall into two groups: first, the Arvanites who settled in Attica, the Peloponnese and elsewhere in the 14th–15th centuries, who speak an ancient Albanian dialect but have mostly integrated into Greek society and switched to Greek; second, the large number of new immigrants who arrived after the fall of Albania's communist regime in the 1990s, who were for a time the largest foreign immigrant group in Greece.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Turkish is used mainly by the Muslim minority of Western Thrace. The Treaty of Lausanne of 1923 exempted them from the population exchange so that they remained in Greece, and the region still has minority schools that teach bilingually in Turkish and Greek.

language.history: The history of Greek spans more than three thousand years, from the Mycenaean Linear B and the Attic dialect of the classical period, to the "Koine Greek" that became the lingua franca of the eastern Mediterranean after Alexander the Great's campaigns, in which the New Testament was written. In the Byzantine period Greek was the official language of the empire, and under Ottoman rule it absorbed a good deal of Turkish and Italian vocabulary. After independence in 1830 the language dispute continued for over a hundred years, until 1976 when modern Demotic Greek was established as the standard. Today Greek is the mother tongue of the vast majority of the country.

ranking.name: Moussaka
ranking.description: Slices of fried or grilled eggplant and tomato-stewed minced beef or lamb are stacked in layers, covered on top with a thick béchamel sauce, and baked until golden.
ranking.history: The name comes from Arabic, and similar eggplant dishes exist throughout the Ottoman Empire and the Middle East. The key to today's Greek version, the béchamel on top, was added in the 1920s by the Greek chef Nikolaos Tselementes, who had trained in France and worked to "remove the Oriental character" of Greek cuisine and bring it closer to Western European cooking. His cookbook was highly influential, making this version the national standard, and today moussaka is a classic dish in Greek restaurants and at Sunday family meals.

ranking.name: Souvlaki
ranking.description: Marinated pieces of pork, chicken or lamb are skewered and charcoal-grilled, and eaten as is or in pita bread, with tzatziki and onion and tomato.
ranking.history: Grilling meat on skewers existed in ancient Greece, the Homeric epics describe warriors roasting sacrificial meat on spits, and archaeology has found ancient grill stands. Modern souvlaki became a cheap fast food on the streets of Athens in the mid-20th century, served with pita and yogurt sauce so that people could eat as they walked. Today it is Greece's most common street snack and a classic late-night meal after evening gatherings.

ranking.name: Greek salad (horiatiki)
ranking.description: Tomato, cucumber, red onion, green pepper and Kalamata olives are cut in large pieces, topped with a whole slab of feta cheese, drizzled with olive oil and sprinkled with oregano.
ranking.history: The Greek name means "village salad", a simple dish that farm families eat in summer. Tomatoes are native to the Americas and were not widely grown in Greece until the 19th century, so the history of this salad is shorter than one might imagine; after the mid-20th century it became a symbol of Greek food with the rise of tourism. Olives and olive oil have been important Greek products since antiquity, and feta cheese gained EU protected designation of origin in the 2000s, so that only that produced in specific regions of Greece may use the name.

ranking.name: Spanakopita (spinach pie)
ranking.description: Many paper-thin layers of phyllo pastry are filled with spinach, feta cheese, spring onion and herbs such as dill, and baked until crisp and golden; it can be eaten hot or cold.
ranking.history: Pies made of layered thin dough were popular in both the Byzantine and Ottoman periods, and the Epirus region of north-western Greece is especially known for its various "pita", where local herders made pies with wild greens, cheese and homemade dough. During the Orthodox Great Lent people make vegetarian versions without cheese and eggs. Today spanakopita is a common breakfast and snack in Greek bakeries and homes, and a must at picnics and gatherings.

ranking.name: Gyros
ranking.description: Layers of marinated meat stacked on a vertical rotating spit are roasted, and thin slices are shaved off and rolled into pita with tomato, onion and tzatziki.
ranking.history: The vertical rotisserie meat derives from the Ottoman Empire's "döner" of the 19th century; after the Greco-Turkish War of 1922–1923, large numbers of Greek refugees from Asia Minor came to Greece and brought this way of roasting meat with them. It became popular in Athens in the mid-20th century, and from the 1970s Greeks replaced the Turkish name with the Greek word "gyros" (turning). It is Greece's most popular fast food and has spread to Europe and America with immigrants.
